newsitem.title: INDIA: Greenpeace protests in India at waste dumping.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace protests in India at waste dumping.

text.p: Environmentalists from more than 10 countries demonstrated in the Indian capital on Thursday against the dumping of toxic industrial by-products by rich nations in Asian countries.

Activists of the international environmental group Greenpeace as well as other national and global organisations, demonstrated outside India's Environment Ministry, shouting slogans and waving banners, Greenpeace said in a statement.

"We want countries like the United States and Australia to know we will not tolerate their attempts to continue using developing countries as a dustbin for their toxic wastes," Greenpeace International spokeswoman Malini Morzaria said.
Greenpeace has urged India to ratify the Basel Convention of 1989 that prohibits the export of hazardous waste for recycling.
The protesters handed over a statement signed by environmental groups from 18 countries to India's caretaker Forests and Environment Minister Saifuddin Soz.
"India is aware of the problem," Greenpeace spokeswoman Morzaria quoted Soz as saying when he accepted the document.
"We have accepted the Basel Convention," Soz added. "We will not accept hazardous waste from industrial countries."
Copies were also delivered to the embassies of the United States, Australia, Brazil and Singapore, the statement said.

Greenpeace says Asia is targeted as a dumping ground because more than 100 non-Asian countries have banned toxic waste imports. India is the leading destination for waste exporters followed by Indonesia, Philippines and China.
Morzaria said more than 65 percent of the 15,000 tonnes of toxic lead waste exported to India between April 1996 and January 1997, originated in developed countries.

Only Finland has ratified the Basel convention, which the United States, Australia and many industries in Western nations oppose in the face of support from most G-77 states and European nations, Greenpeace says.
